items.title: The Phillips curve broke down spectacularly in the 1970s
items.claim: Bill Phillips's 1958 paper documented an inverse relationship between UK unemployment and wage inflation. What happened in the 1970s?

options.text: The relationship held perfectly, vindicating Keynesian demand management
The US and UK experienced 'stagflation' — high inflation AND high unemployment simultaneously, which the simple Phillips curve said was impossible
The relationship inverted entirely; lower unemployment led to deflation
Statistical data became unreliable, so no test was possible

items.reveal:
The 1970s combined oil shocks (1973, 1979), wage-price spirals and weak productivity growth. US inflation reached 13.5% in 1980; unemployment was 7.5%. Both up, together.

Milton Friedman and Edmund Phelps had argued in the late 1960s that the long-run Phillips curve was vertical at the 'natural rate' of unemployment — once expectations adjusted, only the natural rate was stable. The 1970s vindicated them and supplied the intellectual ammunition for monetarism, Volcker and Thatcher.

Modern expectations-augmented Phillips curves are still used but are far less crisp than the original.
items.why: The Phillips curve example is the cleanest case of a model that worked, then didn't. It's also why mid-20th-century Keynesianism gave way to monetarism, with consequences that still shape macro policy.

items.title: The zero lower bound isn't quite zero
items.claim: Conventional theory said nominal interest rates couldn't go below zero because cash would dominate negative-rate deposits. What happened in the 2010s?

options.text: Swiss National Bank, ECB, Bank of Japan, Sveriges Riksbank all set negative deposit rates from 2014-16; commercial banks initially absorbed the cost rather than charging retail depositors, due to fear of bank runs and competitive pressure
All countries banned negative rates by law

items.reveal:
Swiss National Bank cut to -0.75% in January 2015. Negative rates persisted in Europe until 2022. The 'effective' lower bound — where negative rates do more harm than good through bank profitability and disintermediation — turned out to be a soft, country-specific constraint rather than a hard zero.

The alternative tools (QE, forward guidance, yield curve control) became more central to monetary policy at the ZLB, raising questions about the toolkit when conventional rate cuts have less room.
items.why: Constraints that look hard in theory often turn out to be empirical and institutional. The ZLB shaped a decade of unconventional monetary policy.

items.title: The impossible trinity constrains exchange rate policy
items.claim: Robert Mundell's impossible trinity (or trilemma) states that a country cannot simultaneously have:

options.text: A fixed exchange rate, free capital movement, and an independent monetary policy. It must choose two of three

items.reveal:
Mundell's 1963 paper formalised the trilemma. Choices: fix exchange rate + free capital (give up monetary policy: e.g., classical gold standard, eurozone for individual members); free capital + monetary policy (give up fixed rate: US, UK, Japan); fix exchange rate + monetary policy (give up free capital: China, partly).

The ERM crisis (1992) and the Asian financial crisis (1997-98) both showed the cost of trying to maintain all three. Helene Rey's 2015 work argues that with global financial cycles, even floating exchange rates don't fully restore monetary independence — making the trilemma effectively a dilemma.
items.why: Exchange rate policy isn't a free choice; it's a constrained one. The trilemma sets the menu countries can choose from.
